title: Joule Heating: How a Resistor Turns Current into Heat
topic: Joule heating in a resistor — every charge crossing a resistor drops potential V·q which becomes heat; instantaneous power P = V·I = I²R = V²/R; total dissipated energy W = P·t accumulates linearly while the current flows

beats.narration: Current flows through a resistor — where does the energy actually go?

elements.content: Current through a resistor — where does the energy go?

beats.narration: Each charge that crosses the resistor drops by V volts, so it gives up an amount of energy equal to V times q. That energy doesn't vanish — it jiggles the lattice and the resistor warms.

elements.content: Battery on the left, wire loop, resistor as a zigzag in the centre; heat glow on the resistor brightens as time advances
Charge dots stream through the loop and dim as they pass through the resistor
V across the resistor, label and bracket
every charge that crosses leaves a little heat behind

beats.narration: Multiply V times q over time — that's V times I, the power dissipated. Ohm's law gives two more forms: I squared R, and V squared over R. Same wattage, three faces.

elements.content: Substitution arrows: V = IR feeds the middle and right forms
use whichever two quantities you know

beats.narration: Power is the rate, not the total. Energy is power times time — keep the current flowing and the heat piles up, joule by joule, second by second.

elements.content: Horizontal axis: t; vertical axis: W = P·t
Linear line W = P·t rises from the origin as time advances
Moving (t, W) point sliding up the line

beats.narration: It's not loss — it's transformation. A resistor's job is to convert electrical energy into heat.

elements.content: Electrical energy → heat. Not loss — transformation.
(the same physics that boils a kettle and toasts your bread)
